title: Token-Aging Shepherd: priority-based degrade-and-recover for OOM prevention
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We continue to see transient OOMs under mixed workload shapes where long-context, high-concurrency requests consume KV working set and aggressive continuous batching pushes memory over the device headroom. Existing slab-eviction + fallback policies are reactive and often result in high tail latency or degraded output quality when model swaps happen mid-request.

Goal: Implement a proactive, per-request token priority and aging controller ("Token-Aging Shepherd") that coordinates graceful degradation (prefix trimming, fidelity drop, and micro-model hedging) with non-blocking KV operations to avoid hard OOMs while minimizing quality regressions and latency spikes.
technical_design:
High level: Token-Aging Shepherd assigns a compact per-request priority vector (priority score + age counter + opt-in fidelity flag) at admission time. The controller is a lightweight in-memory policy that integrates with the batch admission layer, KV manager, and model router to do three things: 1) Preferentially reserve KV slots for high-priority/young requests; 2) Enforce progressive prefix-trim annealing for lower-priority/aging requests; 3) Trigger hedged execution to a quantized micro-replica or smaller model variant when reservation would breach headroom.

Key components:
- Admission annotator: tags incoming requests with priority (derived from token_count, client_tier, SLA hint, and explicit request_priority header).
- Token aging bucket: every admitted request increments an age label on its KV entries; the controller periodically computes an age-weighted eviction score.
- Non-blocking eviction pipeline: when projected headroom < threshold, the controller issues async KV dematerialize operations (snapshot & soft-evict) for lowest-score entries and signals batch admission to contract batch windows for affected GPUs. Dematerialize returns a compact snapshot reference that can be rehydrated without full cold-start overhead.
- Prefix-trim annealer: for requests flagged as degradable, we apply incremental prefix trimming heuristics (not hard cut) during decode: trim non-topk tokens in oldest context slices and communicate trimmed range to KV manager for eviction precedence.
- Hedging orchestrator: if reservation still risks breach, spawn a concurrent hedged request to pre-warmed smaller/quantized model (micro-replica) with early-merge policy: use first response meeting token-confidence threshold and cancel other in-flight decode.

Dataflow notes: The controller exposes a small telemetry endpoint for per-GPU projected_headroom, reserved_tokens, and dematerialize_queue length. Admission uses this feedback to reject/trim or hedge. All dematerialize ops are idempotent and non-blocking to avoid stalls.

Edge cases and safeguards:
- Never prefix-trim for requests with explicit do_not_trim flag (enterprise customers, audit logs).
- Hedged micro-replicas have strict rate limits to avoid swapping one OOM for many.
- Dematerialize snapshots have TTL and are prioritised for rehydration when re-requested by the same client to preserve coherence.
tradeoffs_and_alternatives:
Alternatives considered: 1) More aggressive synchronous eviction on threshold (rejected because it stalls in-flight decodes and increases tail latency); 2) Global batch throttling (coarse, harms high-priority latency); 3) Per-model static quotas (insufficient for mixed-context workloads).

Trade-offs: Token-Aging Shepherd adds complexity to admission and KV paths and introduces extra metadata overhead (small). Benefits are targeted graceful degradation and fewer hard OOMs. There's an increased risk of subtle correctness bugs around dematerialize/rehydrate; we'll mitigate with conservative defaults and a staged rollout.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Reduction in hard OOM incidents >= 80% for canary region under mixed workload synthetic test harness.
2) Median tail latency increase <= 5% for P0 clients (measured across 95/99p).
3) Quality regression (perplexity or task-specific eval) on degraded paths bounded and tracked; for chat generation tasks, automated eval score drop <= 6% relative.
4) Telemetry shows dematerialize path activation behind projected headroom threshold and hedged micro-replica fallbacks engage only when predicted breach.
5) No data loss: rehydration restores snapshots with consistent tokens for requests reissued within snapshot TTL.
implementation_plan:
Phase 1 (spike, 2w): implement admission annotator and token-aging bucket prototype; add lightweight projected_headroom telemetry. Run offline simulations with captured production traces to tune scores.
Phase 2 (canary, 3w): wire non-blocking dematerialize and prefix-trim annealer for degradable requests; enable hedging to pre-warmed micro-replica pool with conservative rate limits. Deploy to canary cluster (2 GPUs per region) and run chaos tests.
Phase 3 (gradual rollout, 4w): increase traffic 10% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback gates; add rollout knob in Console to opt-in by customer/org.
Phase 4 (hardening): expand micro-replica autoscale, increase dematerialize TTL heuristics, add fine-grained observability and forensics dashboard.

Implementation tasks (examples):
- ENG: admission annotator + metadata plumbing (Diego)
- ENG: token-aging bucket and eviction scoring (Marina)
- ENG: async dematerialize/rehydrate ops (Sanjay)
- ENG: prefix-trim annealer integration in decoder (Lina)
- ENG: hedging orchestrator and micro-replica pool control (Diego/Sara)
- QA: chaos and synthetic trace validation (QA team)
- Observability: console telemetry and SLO alerts (Observability team)
test_plan:
Unit tests for score calculation and idempotency of dematerialize. Integration tests: simulate bursts with long-context sessions to assert dematerialize + rehydrate correctness and hedged early-merge selection. Chaos tests: random GPU OOM injection and verify controller reduces hard OOMs and hedging recovers requests. Performance tests: A/B traffic to measure latency/quality trade-offs.

Synthetic harness: replay recorded prod traces with variables: concurrency, context length, client tiers, and configured headroom. Measure: OOM count, median/95/99 latency, token throughput, hedged fallback rate, and rehydrate success rate.
monitoring_and_metrics:
Primary metrics: hard_oom_count, dematerialize_invocations, rehydrate_success_rate, hedged_fallback_rate, median_latency_p0, p95_latency_p0, quality_drop_degraded_path.
SLOs: hard_oom_count reduced by 80% on canary; hedged_fallback_rate < 3% of requests; rehydrate_success_rate > 99.9%.
Dashboards: per-GPU heads-up showing projected_headroom, dematerialize_queue, age-distribution of KV entries, recent hedged merges, and top offending clients. Alerts: projected_headroom < critical_threshold (auto-contract admission), dematerialize queue growth alarm.
risks:
- Incorrect scoring could evict hot entries and increase downstream latency; mitigate with conservative thresholds and warmup.
- Hedging increases upstream request duplication; mitigate with strict rate limits and early-merge heuristics.
- Dematerialize/rehydrate correctness visible only under rare rehydration paths; ensure thorough end-to-end tests and telemetry.
- Enterprise customers may need explicit exemptions (do_not_trim) — ensure policy respected across control plane/ACLs.
rollout_notes: Start with non-production canary orgs and opt-in internal teams. Expose per-org knob to set degrade_tolerance and hedging budget. Use gradual traffic ramp and automated rollback on quality regression or latency SLO breach. Plan a postmortem if hedged_fallback_rate exceeds 5% for more than 2h.
notes: This approach complements existing slab-eviction and KV compression improvements — it is request-aware rather than purely memory-first. The 'age' signal lets the system prioritize recent interactive sessions and reduces user-visible regressions.
